meta.title: Nerve Tissue
meta.summary: A complex network of nerves and cells that carry messages to and from the brain and spinal cord and various parts of the body.

blocks.name: Nervous system
blocks.def: A complex network of nerves and cells that carry messages to and from the brain and spinal cord and various parts of the body.

blocks.name: Central nervous system (CNS)
blocks.def: The brain and spinal cord; the body's integrating and command center; protected by bones, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and the meninges.

blocks.name: Peripheral nervous system (PNS)
blocks.def: Everything outside the CNS; consists of cranial and spinal nerves, plus associated ganglia (sensory ganglia, cranial nerve ganglia, autonomic ganglia).

blocks.name: Neurons (nerve cells)
blocks.def: Excitable cells that transmit electrical signals; the basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system.

blocks.name: Neuroglia (glial cells)
blocks.def: Nonexcitable supporting cells with branching processes and a central cell body. Outnumber neurons roughly 10 to 1, make up about half the mass of the brain, and — unlike most neurons — can divide throughout life.

blocks.name: Glioma
blocks.def: A tumor arising from glial cells.

blocks.name: Neuron (special characteristics)
blocks.def: Longevity — can live and function for a lifetime. Amitotic — cannot be replaced if destroyed in most circumstances (exceptions include the olfactory <term d="The sheet of tightly packed cells that covers surfaces and lines cavities and tubes.">epithelium</term> of the nose and certain hippocampal regions involved in memory). High metabolic rate — requires abundant oxygen and glucose; neurons die after about 5 minutes without oxygen.

blocks.name: Cell body (soma / perikaryon)
blocks.def: The metabolic center of the neuron, 5–140 μm in diameter, containing the usual organelles plus chromatophilic bodies and neurofibrils.

blocks.name: Chromatophilic bodies (<term d="Clumps of rough endoplasmic reticulum in a neuron's cell body, where its proteins are made.">Nissl bodies</term>)
blocks.def: Clusters of rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes within the neuron cell body; stain darkly and are responsible for renewing the cell's membranes.

blocks.name: Neurofibrils
blocks.def: Bundles of intermediate filaments that form a network between the chromatophilic bodies of a neuron.

blocks.name: Neuronal pigments
blocks.def: Some neurons contain pigments in their cell body, such as black melanin, an iron-containing red pigment, or a gold-brown pigment called lipofuscin.

blocks.name: Location of neuron cell bodies
blocks.def: Most neuronal cell bodies are located in the CNS, protected by the bones of the skull and vertebral column.

blocks.name: Nuclei vs. ganglia
blocks.def: Nuclei are clusters of neuron cell bodies in the CNS; ganglia are clusters of neuron cell bodies in the PNS, lying along peripheral nerves.

blocks.name: Tracts vs. nerves
blocks.def: In the CNS, bundles of neuron processes are called tracts. In the PNS, these bundles are called nerves.

blocks.name: Nerve impulse
blocks.def: An electrochemical change transmitted by neurons to other neurons and to cells outside the nervous system.

blocks.name: Dendrites
blocks.def: Extensively branching processes from the cell body that function as receptive sites, receiving signals from other neurons and transmitting electrical signals toward the cell body. Chromatophilic bodies only extend into the basal part of dendrites.

blocks.name: <term d="The long single process of a neuron that carries signals away from the cell body.">Axon</term>
blocks.def: A long, slender <term d="A movement that increases the angle at a joint, straightening it.">extension</term> from the soma, emerging at the axon hillock. Each neuron has only one axon (though it may have branches called axon collaterals); may be myelinated or unmyelinated; lacks chromatophilic bodies and does no protein synthesis; transmits impulses away from the cell body.

blocks.name: Axon hillock
blocks.def: The point where the axon emerges from the soma.

blocks.name: Axon collaterals
blocks.def: Occasional branches off the main axon.

blocks.name: Axon organelle content
blocks.def: Axons have the same organelles as dendrites, except for rough endoplasmic reticulum and a Golgi apparatus — which is why they decay quickly if cut or severely damaged.

blocks.name: Telodendria (terminal branches)
blocks.def: Multiple branches at the very end of an axon.

blocks.name: Axon terminals (synaptic terminals / boutons)
blocks.def: Knob-like endings of the telodendria, containing synaptic vesicles specialized for releasing neurotransmitters.

blocks.name: <term d="The junction where one nerve cell passes its signal on to the next cell.">Synapse</term>
blocks.def: The site of functional contact between a neuron and another neuron, an effector cell, or a sensory receptor cell; signals pass across a synapse in one direction only.

blocks.name: Presynaptic neuron
blocks.def: The neuron that conducts a signal toward a synapse.

blocks.name: Postsynaptic neuron
blocks.def: The neuron that transmits electrical activity away from a synapse.

blocks.name: Synaptic vesicles
blocks.def: Membrane-bound sacs on the presynaptic side of a synapse, containing neurotransmitters.

blocks.name: Synaptic cleft
blocks.def: The actual gap between neurons, separating the plasma membranes of the pre- and postsynaptic neurons.

blocks.name: Neuromuscular junction
blocks.def: A synapse between a neuron and a muscle cell.

blocks.name: Axodendritic synapse
blocks.def: A synapse between the axon terminals of one neuron and the dendrites of another — the most common synapse type.

blocks.name: Axosomatic synapse
blocks.def: A synapse between an axon and a neuronal cell body.

blocks.name: Other synapse types
blocks.def: Axoaxonic (axon-to-axon), dendrodendritic (dendrite-to-dendrite), and dendrosomatic (dendrite-to-cell-body) synapses — all relatively uncommon.

blocks.name: Multipolar neurons
blocks.def: Numerous dendrites and one axon; the most abundant neuron type, making up about 99% of neurons.

blocks.name: Bipolar neurons
blocks.def: Rare neurons with one <term d="A branching process of a neuron that receives signals and carries them toward the cell body.">dendrite</term> and one axon; found in some special sensory organs (inner ear, olfactory epithelium, retina), mostly serving as sensory neurons.

blocks.name: Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons
blocks.def: Cell bodies located in ganglia outside the CNS; the central process runs into the CNS while the peripheral process extends to the receptors. Start as bipolar neurons during development. Serve as sensory neurons of the PNS, found in spinal and cranial nerve ganglia.

blocks.name: Sensory (afferent) neurons
blocks.def: Transmit impulses from tissues and organs toward the CNS; virtually all are unipolar neurons.

blocks.name: Motor (efferent) neurons
blocks.def: Carry impulses away from the CNS to effector organs; most are multipolar, with cell bodies within the CNS, forming junctions with effectors (muscles and glands).

blocks.name: Somatic motor neurons
blocks.def: Motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscle.

blocks.name: Visceral motor neurons (ANS)
blocks.def: Autonomic motor neurons that innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.

blocks.name: Interneurons (association neurons)
blocks.def: Mostly multipolar; lie between motor and sensory neurons, confined entirely to the CNS; make up about 99.98% of all neurons in the body.

blocks.name: The 6 types of neuroglia
blocks.def: 4 found in the CNS (astrocytes, microglia, ependymal cells, oligodendrocytes) and 2 found in the PNS (satellite cells, Schwann cells).

blocks.name: General functions of neuroglia
blocks.def: Surround neurons and hold them in place; supply nutrients and oxygen; insulate one neuron from another; destroy and remove dead neurons; repair neuronal injury; regulate the CNS's internal fluid environment; clear neurotransmitters from synaptic clefts; and mediate metabolic exchange between the vascular system and neurons.

blocks.name: Astrocytes
blocks.def: Star-shaped, the largest and most abundant glial cell type; found between neurons and blood vessels, anchoring them together. Contribute to the blood-brain barrier, control capillary blood flow, absorb/recycle neurotransmitters, assist synapse formation in developing tissue, produce neuronal growth factors (like BDNF), and regulate sodium, potassium, and CO₂ concentrations.

blocks.name: Microglia
blocks.def: The smallest and least abundant glial cell; act as the phagocytes (macrophages) of the CNS; appear early in embryonic development; derived from blood cells called monocytes.

blocks.name: Ependymal cells
blocks.def: Line the central canal of the spinal cord and the ventricles of the brain; help form the choroid plexuses that secrete cerebrospinal fluid (CSF); bear <term d="Short hair-like projections that beat in waves to sweep fluid or particles along a surface.">cilia</term> that help circulate the CSF.

blocks.name: Oligodendrocytes
blocks.def: "Few-branch cells" that form the myelin sheaths around axons in the CNS; have multiple processes and can coil around several different axons at once.

blocks.name: Satellite cells (amphicytes)
blocks.def: PNS glial cells with functions similar to astrocytes; surround and protect neuron cell bodies within ganglia.

blocks.name: Schwann cells (neurolemmocytes)
blocks.def: Form the myelin sheath and neurolemma (sheath of Schwann) around axons in the PNS; surround only a single axon.

blocks.name: Neurolemma
blocks.def: The <term d="Closer to the surface of the body.">superficial</term> cytoplasmic covering provided by Schwann cells; provides a regeneration tube that guides regrowth of a severed axon.

blocks.name: Myelin
blocks.def: Multilayered lipids and proteins forming a sheath around certain nerve fibers, formed by oligodendrocytes in the CNS and Schwann cells in the PNS. Forms an insulating layer, prevents leakage of electrical current from the axon, and increases the speed of impulse conduction. Thicker axons are myelinated; thin axons are unmyelinated and conduct impulses more slowly.

blocks.name: Multiple sclerosis
blocks.def: A demyelination disease.

blocks.name: Nodes of Ranvier
blocks.def: Gaps in the myelin sheath along an axon in the PNS, where the myelin sheath is not continuous.

blocks.name: Gray matter
blocks.def: Contains neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axons, axon terminals, and neuroglia. Appears grayish (rather than white) because Nissl bodies impart a gray color and there is little or no myelin present.

blocks.name: White matter
blocks.def: Composed primarily of myelinated axons; the whitish colour of myelin gives white matter its name.

blocks.name: Endoneurium
blocks.def: A layer of delicate <term d="The tissue that supports, binds and separates other tissues, rich in matrix between its cells.">connective tissue</term> surrounding an individual axon.

blocks.name: Perineurium
blocks.def: Connective tissue wrapping surrounding a nerve fascicle (a bundle of axons).

blocks.name: Nerve fascicles
blocks.def: Groups of axons bound together into bundles.

blocks.name: Epineurium
blocks.def: The tough, fibrous sheath surrounding a whole nerve.

blocks.name: Neural plasticity
blocks.def: The nervous system's capability to change based on experience — via sprouting of new dendrites, synthesis of new proteins, and changes in synaptic contacts with other neurons.

blocks.name: Nervous system maturation
blocks.def: Continues through childhood, reflecting the progressive myelination and thickening of axons.

blocks.name: Limited neuronal regeneration
blocks.def: Mammalian neurons have very limited powers of regeneration (the capability to replicate or repair damaged neurons).

blocks.name: CNS repair (or lack thereof)
blocks.def: In the CNS, little or no repair of neuronal damage occurs — even when the cell body remains intact, a severed axon cannot be repaired or regrown. Astrocytes produce scar tissue that blocks axon growth across the damaged area and release chemicals that further block axon regrowth.

blocks.name: PNS repair
blocks.def: Axons and dendrites associated with a neurolemma in the PNS may undergo repair if the cell body is intact, the Schwann cells are functional, and scar tissue formation does not occur too rapidly.

blocks.name: Chromatolysis
blocks.def: The breakup of Nissl bodies into fine granular masses, occurring about 1–2 days after injury to a peripheral neuron's process.

blocks.name: Wallerian degeneration
blocks.def: The degeneration of the <term d="Further away from the trunk or from the point where a limb attaches.">distal</term> portion of an injured axon and its myelin sheath (occurring by the 3rd–5th day post-injury), while macrophages phagocytize the debris and the neurolemma remains intact.

blocks.name: Regeneration tube
blocks.def: A tube formed when Schwann cells on either side of an injury site multiply by mitosis and grow toward each other, guiding the growth of a new axon from the <term d="Nearer to the trunk or to the point where a limb attaches.">proximal</term> area across the injury into the distal area previously occupied by the original axon.

blocks.name: Limits of axon regrowth
blocks.def: New axons will not grow if the gap at the injury site is too large, or if the gap becomes filled with <term d="A strong rope-like protein fibre that gives tissues their tensile strength.">collagen</term> fibers. Regenerating axons grow toward their distal targets at roughly 1.5 mm per day.
